library(tidyverse)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 8,

  out.width = "90%",

# Problem 1

```{r birthday-function}
birthday_repeated = function(n) {

  birthdays = sample(
    1:365,
    size = n,
    replace = TRUE
  )

  repeated = length(unique(birthdays)) < n

  return(repeated)
}
```

```{r birthday-simulation}
birthday_results_df =
  expand_grid(
    group_size = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    repeated = map_lgl(group_size, birthday_repeated)
  )

birthday_prob_df =
  birthday_results_df |>
  group_by(group_size) |>
  summarize(
    prob_repeat = mean(repeated),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

birthday_prob_df
```

```{r birthday-plot}
birthday_prob_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = prob_repeat)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of Shared Birthdays by Group Size",
    x = "Group Size",
    y = "Probability of Shared Birthdays"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    labels = scales::percent
  )
```

The probability that at least two people share a birthday increases as group size increases. 
The relationship is nonlinear, with the probability increasing rapidly for smaller group sizes 
before gradually approaching 1. The probability exceeds approximately 50% when the group contains 23 people. 
This illustrates the birthday paradox, where shared birthdays become surprisingly likely even in relatively small groups.

# Problem 2

```{r import-data}
file_names =
  tibble(
    file_name = list.files(
      path = "./data",
      pattern = "\\.csv$",
      full.names = TRUE
    )
  )

file_names
```

```{r read-data}
study_df =
  file_names |>
  mutate(
    data = map(file_name, read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)
  )

study_df
```

```{r tidy-data}
study_tidy_df =
  study_df |>
  mutate(
    arm = case_when(
      str_detect(file_name, "con_") ~ "Control",
      str_detect(file_name, "exp_") ~ "Experimental"
    ),
    subject_id = str_extract(
      basename(file_name), "\\d+"
    )
  ) |>
  select(-file_name) |>
  unnest(data) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    week = as.numeric(str_remove(week, "week_")),
    arm = factor(
      arm,
      levels = c("Control", "Experimental")
    )
  ) |>
  arrange(arm, subject_id, week)

study_tidy_df
```

```{r spaghetti-plot}
study_tidy_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = week,
      y = observation,
      group = interaction(arm, subject_id),
      color = arm
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_grid(. ~ arm) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly Observations by Treatment Arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Treatment Arm"
  )
```

The spaghetti plot shows different longitudinal patterns between the control and experimental groups. 
Observations in the control group remain relatively stable across the eight weeks, 
with some individual variability. In contrast, participants in the experimental group 
generally show increasing observations over time. Although there is variation across individuals, 
the upward trend in the experimental group suggests a positive effect of the experimental intervention 
on the measured outcome. However, since we did not conduct a hypothesis test, 
this descriptive comparison alone does not establish statistical significance.

# Problem 3

```{r simulation-function}
sim_ttest = function(mu, n = 30, sigma = 5) {

  sim_data = tibble(
    x = rnorm(
      n = n,
      mean = mu,
      sd = sigma
    )
  )

  test_results =
    t.test(sim_data$x, mu = 0) |>
    broom::tidy()

  test_results |>
    select(estimate, p.value)
}
```

```{r run-simulation}
sim_results_df =
  expand_grid(
    mu = 0:6,
    iter = 1:5000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    test_results = map(mu, sim_ttest)
  ) |>
  unnest(test_results) |>
  mutate(
    reject = p.value < 0.05
  )

sim_results_df
```

```{r power-summary}
power_df =
  sim_results_df |>
  group_by(mu) |>
  summarize(
    power = mean(reject),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

power_df
```

```{r power-plot}
power_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = power)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    labels = scales::percent
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Statistical Power by True Mean",
    x = "True Mean (mu)",
    y = "Proportion of Null Hypotheses Rejected"
  )
```

The probability of rejecting the null hypothesis increases as the true mean increases from 0 to 6. 
When the true mean is 0, the rejection proportion is approximately 0.05, consistent with 
the nominal Type I error rate. As the true mean moves further away from the null value, 
the effect size increases relative to the fixed standard deviation, making it easier 
to detect a statistically significant difference. Consequently, statistical power increases 
and approaches 1 for larger values of the true mean.

```{r estimate-summary}
estimate_df =
  sim_results_df |>
  group_by(mu) |>
  summarize(
    mean_estimate = mean(estimate),
    mean_estimate_rejected =
      mean(estimate[reject]),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

estimate_df
```

```{r estimate-plot}
estimate_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = mu, y = mean_estimate)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimate by True Mean",
    x = "True Mean (mu)",
    y = "Average Estimate of mu"
  )
```

```{r estimate-comparison-plot}
estimate_df |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      mean_estimate,
      mean_estimate_rejected
    ),
    names_to = "estimate_type",
    values_to = "average_estimate"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    estimate_type = recode(
      estimate_type,
      mean_estimate = "All Samples",
      mean_estimate_rejected = "Rejected Samples Only"
    )
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = mu,
      y = average_estimate,
      color = estimate_type
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimates Across All and Rejected Samples",
    x = "True Mean (mu)",
    y = "Average Estimated Mean",
    color = "Sample Selection"
  )
```

The average estimates across all simulated samples are approximately equal to the true mean, 
consistent with the unbiasedness of the sample mean. However, when considering only samples 
in which the null hypothesis was rejected, the average estimated mean tends to be larger than the true mean,
particularly for small positive effect sizes.
This difference arises from selection bias. When the true effect is small, samples with unusually 
large positive estimates are more likely to produce statistically significant results. 
Restricting the analysis to significant results therefore overrepresents larger estimates 
and can exaggerate the magnitude of the true effect. As the true mean increases, 
statistical power approaches 1, meaning that nearly all samples reject the null hypothesis. 
Consequently, the difference between the average estimates from all samples and rejected samples becomes smaller.
When the true mean is 0, statistically significant estimates can occur in both positive and negative directions, 
so their average may still be close to 0. Overall, these results illustrate how selecting estimates 
based on statistical significance can lead to exaggerated effect sizes, especially when statistical power is low.
